title: Rip Van Winkle

teacherSummary.text: Good-natured, idle Rip Van Winkle wanders into the Catskill Mountains to escape his scolding wife, meets strange men in old Dutch dress playing ninepins, drinks their liquor, and falls asleep. He wakes twenty years later, bearded and stiff. In the village, King George's portrait has become George Washington, his wife is dead, and the Revolution has happened. He settles into old age telling his story.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “petticoat government” slowly and put it in my own words: Rip, back from his long sleep, rejoices that his wife is dead and he is no longer ruled at home. Next, craft. I notice the joking mix of words: "government," a political term, applied to a marriage. The strongest word is “petticoat”: a petticoat is a woman's underskirt, so the phrase mocks rule by a wife. Then, effect. Why is Rip glad to be free from "petticoat government"? My answer: Rip is glad to be free from "petticoat government" because his wife has died; he slept through a revolution, but the only tyranny he cares about escaping was hers, a joke showing he has not changed.
